## 4.1 Conceptual framework

Numerous studies have established that the performance of Ghanaian farmers is influenced by various factors, including geographical location [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2021b; @Tsiboe2022], farmer's age [@Asravor2024], and gender [@Adaku2022], among others. In the context of this study, we conceptualize agricultural service delivery as a community-level institutional environment that may shape smallholder farm performance through two related channels: technical efficiency and access to superior production technologies. Technical efficiency reflects how well farmers convert available inputs into output relative to the production frontier available to their group, while the technology gap ratio captures how close that group-specific frontier is to the best feasible production frontier available to all farmers in the sample. The decomposition is the meta-frontier framework's [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008].

Separating the two channels is the point of the exercise, because they carry different policy content. A community whose farmers are technically efficient but whose frontier lies well below the meta-frontier has an access problem: the practices are being used well, but they are not the best practices available. A community whose frontier is close to the meta-frontier but whose farmers sit well inside it has a utilisation problem instead. A single measure of productivity cannot distinguish these, and the two call for different responses. The empirical question of this paper is which of the two, if either, moves with the presence of agricultural service delivery.

The main empirical specification uses access to any agricultural service source to classify farmers into two technology groups: farmers in communities with at least one agricultural service source, and farmers in communities without any identified source. This grouping reflects the idea that communities with agricultural services may operate under a different production environment from communities without such services. Services can raise within-group technical efficiency by helping farmers use land, labor, seed, fertilizer, pesticides, and other inputs more effectively. They can also narrow technology gaps, by improving access to better practices, input information, mechanization support, credit, irrigation knowledge, post-harvest support, and market-related services. Farmers exposed to agricultural services may then be closer both to their own group frontier and to the meta-frontier. The Ghanaian evidence supports both readings without settling between them: studies of cereal, vegetable, legume and starchy-staple systems report technical inefficiency responding to extension exposure and to the managerial and demographic characteristics that mediate it [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2022; @Asravor2024; @Ansah2023], while the technology-gap literature finds accessible technology sets differing systematically across groups defined by exactly this kind of institutional access [@Adaku2022; @Tsiboe2021b].

Agricultural service delivery is not a single-channel intervention. Services reach farmers through agricultural or fishing associations, through agricultural cooperatives, or through active extension delivery, and the three work differently. Associations support coordination, information exchange, input access, communal labor, and marketing. Cooperatives bear on bargaining power, on access to services, and on collective action. Extension delivers technical advice and farmer-facing guidance directly. The applied meta-frontier literature has treated each of these as a technology-defining boundary in its own right: seed-variety access in Ghanaian maize [@TweneboahKodua2022], production practice in Ethiopian cereals [@Birhanu2022], and resource endowment in Bangladeshi dairy [@Uddin2014]. This paper adopts the same design for service source. For this reason, in addition to the main specification based on access to any agricultural service source, the study conducts separate analyses using service-source measures to assess whether farm performance differs by the channel through which agricultural support is delivered. Section 2.1 sets out why these three contrasts share a comparison group and are therefore not independent of one another.

The study also considers the content of services available to farmers. Agricultural support may focus on planting or seed use, mechanization or agricultural equipment, credit, irrigation, animal husbandry, fertilizer or agrochemical input use, and post-harvest, marketing, or storage services. The pathways differ. Planting and seed-use advice bears on crop establishment; mechanization relaxes labor and timeliness constraints; credit eases liquidity constraints; irrigation reduces exposure to rainfall variability; husbandry support matters in mixed farming systems; input advice bears on fertilizer and pesticide decisions; and post-harvest or marketing support reduces losses and eases market participation. Content enters the analysis as a disaggregation of the estimated gap rather than as a separate treatment, and Figure 3 reports it that way.

## 4.2 Meta-stochastic frontier analysis

This study examines whether agricultural service delivery is associated with differences in smallholder farm performance in Ghana. The analysis focuses on three related outcomes: technical efficiency, technology gap ratios, and meta-technical efficiency. To estimate these outcomes, we apply the meta-stochastic frontier framework [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008], which allows farmers operating under different service environments to have separate group-specific production frontiers while also being compared to a common meta-frontier. This framework is appropriate because farmers in communities with agricultural service access may face a different production environment from farmers in communities without such access.

In the main specification, farmers are separated into two groups based on whether their community has access to any agricultural service source. The first group consists of farmers in communities with at least one agricultural service source, including agricultural or fishing associations, agricultural cooperatives, or active extension delivery. The second group consists of farmers in communities without any identified agricultural service source. Separate stochastic frontier production functions are estimated for these two groups. The group-specific frontiers provide estimates of technical efficiency, which measure how efficiently each farmer converts input into output relative to other farmers operating in the same service environment.

The group-specific stochastic frontier for farmer $i$, service group $j$, and survey round $t$ is specified as a translog production function:

$f^{j}\left( x_{ijt} \right) = \ln y_{ijt} = \beta_{0j} + \sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{kj}\ln x_{kijt}} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}^{}{\sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{skj}\ln x_{kijt}\ln x_{sijt}}} + \mathbf{\beta}_{h}\mathbf{h}_{ijt} + v_{ijt} - u_{ijt}$

$u_{ijt}\sim N^{+}\left\lbrack 0,\exp\left( \mathbf{w}_{ijt}\mathbf{\alpha} \right) \right\rbrack$, $v_{ijt}\sim N\left( 0,\sigma_{vj}^{2} \right)$ (1)

where $y_{ijt}$ is crop output for farmer $i$ in service group $j$ and survey round $t$. The vector $x_{kijt}$ contains six production inputs: land, planting materials, family labor, hired labor, fertilizer, and pesticide, in that order. The vector $h_{ijt}$ holds the intercept shifters: the shares of cultivated area under each listed crop, the survey round, and the agroecological zone. These allow the level of the frontier to differ across cropping systems, periods and ecologies without allowing its slope to. The term $v_{ijt}$ captures random shocks outside the farmer's control, while $u_{ijt}$ captures technical inefficiency. The inefficiency term is modelled as a function of farmer and farm characteristics $w_{ijt}$: the logarithms of age and years of schooling, crop diversification, and indicators for survey round, gender, agroecological zone, credit access, land ownership and mechanization. Table S7 reports the full frontier and Table S8 the inefficiency function.

Three specification choices deserve a word. We adopt the translog rather than the Cobb-Douglas form for its flexibility. A likelihood-ratio test rejects the Cobb-Douglas restriction decisively on the pooled national frontier (LR = `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$functional_form$naive$lr), 1)` on `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$functional_form$naive$df), 0)` degrees of freedom, p `r ifelse(assert_present(objs$functional_form$naive$p) < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", fmt_num(objs$functional_form$naive$p, 3)))`), and on each group frontier separately; the Cobb-Douglas estimates are reported alongside the other alternatives in Figure S2 so the cost of the choice can be read off directly. We assume a half-normal distribution for the inefficiency term, having found more flexible distributions unstable in the subgroup fits; exponential, generalised-exponential and Rayleigh alternatives are estimated and reported in Figure S2. And the household design weight enters the likelihood, so the frontier describes the population each farmer represents rather than the achieved sample.

Preliminary translog estimates violated the theoretical properties a production function is required to satisfy, as unrestricted translog fits routinely do. We therefore impose monotonicity during estimation and evaluate quasi-concavity afterwards. After correction, monotonicity is satisfied for `r fmt_num(100 * min(unlist(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$mono))), 2)` percent to `r fmt_num(100 * max(unlist(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$mono))), 2)` percent of observations and curvature for `r fmt_num(100 * min(unlist(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$curv))), 2)` percent to `r fmt_num(100 * max(unlist(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$curv))), 2)` percent, depending on the frontier (Table 6). The spread is wide and we do not present it as satisfactory: the meta-frontier satisfies monotonicity almost everywhere, while the served-group frontier satisfies it on well under half its observations, and curvature holds on a minority of observations under every frontier. Estimates that rest on the curvature-violating region should be read with that in mind. The share of total variance attributable to inefficiency rather than noise ranges from `r fmt_num(min(unlist(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$gamma))), 3)` to `r fmt_num(max(unlist(assert_present(objs$diagnostics$gamma))), 3)` across the frontiers, so the inefficiency component is substantial in every specification and the frontier framework is doing real work rather than fitting noise.

Technical efficiency for each farmer is calculated as:

${TE}_{ijt} = \ E\left\lbrack \exp\left( - u_{ijt} \right)|{\widehat{\varepsilon}}_{ijt} \right\rbrack$ (2)

where $TE_{ijt}$ measures the farmer's efficiency relative to the service-group-specific frontier. In this framework the service indicator does not enter as a conventional regression covariate; it defines the group-specific production technology. That is what allows the analysis to ask whether farmers in served communities operate on a different frontier, rather than only whether they sit at a different point on a common one.

In the second step, the estimated group-specific frontiers are enveloped by a common meta-frontier, representing the best feasible production technology available across all farmers in the sample regardless of service environment:

$f^{M}\left( x_{ijt} \right) = \ln{\widehat{y}}_{ijt} = \beta_{0M} + \sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{kM}\ln x_{kiMt}} + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{s}^{}{\sum_{k}^{}{\beta_{skM}\ln x_{kiMt}\ln x_{siMt}}} + \mathbf{\beta}_{h}\mathbf{h}_{ijt} - u_{Mijt}$ (3)

where $u_{Mijt} \geq 0$ captures the distance between the group-specific frontier and the meta-frontier. The technology gap ratio is then defined as:

${TGR}_{ijt} = \frac{f^{j}\left( x_{ijt} \right)}{f^{M}\left( x_{ijt} \right)} = e^{- u_{iM}} \leq 1$ (4)

The technology gap ratio measures how close the production technology available to a farmer's service group is to the best feasible technology represented by the meta-frontier. A value closer to one indicates a smaller technology gap, while a lower value indicates that the group-specific frontier lies further below the meta-frontier.

Meta-technical efficiency combines within-group technical efficiency and the technology gap ratio:

${MTE}_{ijt} = \ f^{j}\left( x_{ijt} \right)\left\lbrack f^{M}\left( x_{ijt} \right)e^{v_{ijt}} \right\rbrack^{- 1} = {TGR}_{ijt} \times {TE}_{ijt}$ (5)

This measure captures each farmer's performance relative to the overall meta-frontier. It reflects both how efficiently the farmer uses available inputs within the service environment and how close that service environment is to the best available production technology. Because MTE is the product of the two, a service source can raise MTE by raising either component, and the three measures must be read together: an improvement in TE offset by a deterioration in TGR leaves MTE unmoved while describing a substantively different situation.

Input elasticities are computed from the first-order partial derivatives of the fitted frontier, evaluated at each observation and averaged with sampling weights; returns to scale are their sum. Reporting them serves a second purpose beyond describing the technology. If service provision operated only by shifting the level of output, the elasticities would be common across groups and only the intercepts would differ; group-specific elasticities are what make the two frontiers genuinely two technologies rather than one technology at two heights. Table 6 reports them for both groups and for the meta-frontier.

Given the differences in sampling, question structure, and implementation across the GLSS rounds, treating the pooled data as a single cross-section would risk masking real variation. Equations (1) to (5) are estimated within survey round, and the efficiency scores and elasticities are averaged across rounds afterwards. Each comparison is thus made between farmers surveyed under the same instrument in the same year, and the pooled figures reported throughout are averages of within-round comparisons rather than comparisons across pooled data.

After estimating the main model, farmer-level technical efficiency, technology gap ratios, and meta-technical efficiency are predicted and summarised across age, gender, education, crop and region, and across the content of services available. This is the basis of Figures 3 to 5. It is descriptive disaggregation of an estimated gap rather than a separate identification strategy, and it is reported as such.

## 4.3 Balanced sample construction

Agricultural services are not randomly distributed across communities. Communities with service access may differ from those without in location, infrastructure, crop mix, commercialization, farmer organization, land ownership, education, and broader institutional capacity, and Section 2.2 shows several of these differences directly. Comparing group-specific frontiers estimated on such samples would confound the technology available to a group with the composition of the group itself. Our empirical strategy rests on a balanced matched sample. The purpose of matching here is not to establish causal effects but to construct a more comparable analytic sample for the meta-stochastic frontier, so that the two frontiers describe farmers who are alike on what we observe. This follows applications of meta-frontier methods in productivity studies where group assignment is associated with observed characteristics [@Mayen2010; @CrespoCebada2014; @Asmare2022; @BravoUreta2021; @Tiedemann2013].

The grouping variable for matching is access to any agricultural service source. This broad measure is used because the service-source and service-content indicators are nested within it, so a single matched sample supports every contrast the paper reports. Farmers are matched on demographic characteristics, namely age, education, marital status, religion, ethnicity, and relationship to the household head; on household size, dependency ratio and female share; and on crop diversification and the share of cultivated area under each listed crop, together with land ownership and credit access. Matching is conducted strictly within strata defined by operator gender, survey round, region, agroecological zone, and rural or urban locality, so that no match crosses a boundary along which the production environment or the instrument itself changes.

Balancing treated and untreated groups across this many continuous and categorical covariates admits no single obvious metric, so we do not choose one a priori. We implement one-to-one nearest-neighbour matching under eight distance specifications: Euclidean and scaled Euclidean distance, Mahalanobis [@Rubin1980] and robust Mahalanobis distance [@Rosenbaum2020], and propensity scores under logit, probit, complementary log-log and Cauchit links. Each is evaluated on standardized mean differences, variance ratios, and Kolmogorov--Smirnov statistics, with optimal balance indicated by standardized differences close to zero and variance ratios close to one [@Rubin2001; @Stuart2010]. Table S6 reports all three diagnostics for every specification together with the composite criterion that ranks them, and Figure S1 reports every specification against every covariate.

Scaled Euclidean distance is used in the main analysis. Two features of that choice should be visible rather than asserted. The distance-based metrics separate from the propensity-score metrics decisively, every propensity-score link being worse on all three diagnostics. They barely separate from each other. Scaled Euclidean and Mahalanobis are indistinguishable on standardized mean differences and differ in the fourth decimal of the composite criterion, so the ranking between the top two is not a finding and nothing in the paper turns on it. Figure S2 reports the estimates under alternative matching metrics. The matched sample retains `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Sample size", "meta_m"), 0)` of the `r fmt_num(tbl_val("table6", "Sample size", "meta_u"), 0)` farm observations. Because matching discards unmatched treated units as well as unmatched controls, the matched sample is not a random subsample of the analysis sample, and results on it describe the region of covariate overlap rather than the full population of Ghanaian crop farmers.

Every estimate in the paper is reported on both samples. Table 6 and Figure 1 carry the matched and unmatched frontiers side by side, so the contribution of matching to each gap can be read off the exhibit rather than taken on trust.

To estimate standard errors we use a jackknife resampling procedure. The correction that imposes monotonicity in Equations (1) and (3) prevents estimation of a conventional variance-covariance matrix, so an analytic standard error is not available. For each survey round we construct 100 resampled datasets, each excluding one enumeration area, and re-run the entire procedure on every one of them: the group-specific frontiers, the matching, and the meta-frontier. The dispersion of the estimates across resamples gives the reported standard errors. This propagates the uncertainty introduced by the matched-sample construction as well as by estimation, which an analytic standard error conditional on the matched sample would not, and it respects the clustering of the survey design by resampling at the level at which the sample was drawn.

## 4.4 What the design identifies

Several limitations bound the interpretation of what follows, and we state them here rather than after the results.

Identification rests on selection on observables. Matching balances the farmer, household and production characteristics listed above within strata defined by gender, round, region, agroecological zone and locality, together with overlap on those characteristics. It cannot address confounding from unobserved determinants of both service provision and farm performance: soil quality, distance to markets and roads, road and electricity infrastructure, household wealth, the strength of local institutions, or the political salience of a community to the agencies that allocate extension staff. The last of these is the sharpest case, because service placement is a decision made by an agency with objectives of its own. If extension is directed toward communities with higher agricultural potential, then service provision and productive capacity are jointly determined by something we do not observe, and the estimated gap will absorb it. Stronger correction would require a valid exclusion restriction, and the GLSS contains no instrument for community service provision that is credibly unrelated to farm performance. We interpret the estimated differences in TGR, TE, and MTE as associations conditional on observables in a balanced sample, not as causal effects of agricultural service delivery. Where the discussion below uses the language of influence or effect, it should be read in that sense.

The treatment is measured at the community level and describes availability, not receipt. A farmer in a served community who never met an extension officer is counted as exposed, and a farmer who sought advice privately in an unserved community is counted as unexposed. This attenuates the estimated gap toward zero relative to the difference between actual participants and non-participants. The size of the attenuation depends on uptake, which the community module does not measure. We know the direction of the bias and not its magnitude.

The stable-unit-treatment-value assumption is not innocuous here and we do not assume it silently. Extension officers, cooperatives and associations operate across community boundaries, farmers in unserved communities may obtain advice from neighbours in served ones, and traders and input dealers move information the same way. Spillover of this kind contaminates the comparison group in the direction of understating the gap. Matching within region and agroecological zone makes matched pairs geographically closer, which if anything increases the risk. We cannot bound this with the data available.

Three further limitations follow from the data. The service measures are harmonized across rounds, so detail available in one round but not another is discarded to preserve comparability, and compliance with advisory guidance is observed in GLSS6 and GLSS7 only. The treatment records the presence of a service source and nothing about its intensity, quality, or duration. A community served for twenty years and one served since last season are coded alike. So are a well-staffed extension office and a nominal one. And the data are repeated cross-sections rather than a panel, so the wave-to-wave patterns describe changing associations across successive samples of farmers, not changes within farmers over time, and they cannot identify the lagged responses through which service provision is theorised to operate.
